Explain jargon as you go: 'price per unit (called NAV)', and 'your ₹10,000 buys more units when prices are low. That's called rupee-cost averaging.' Use buttons that say what you get ('Stay on →'), and use 'Not quite, here's the twist' instead of 'costly mistake!'. (Benchmark #20 Local life events, local money — SEBI Check QR game)

[Kit: WhatsApp share (text) + Share image card] The WhatsApp line shows one emoji per drop (✅ stayed on, ⏸️ paused, 🚪 got off, ➕ topped up) plus the archetype, with no rupee figures. The 9:16 card shows the track with the player's pins on it. Link to the game's own page once it is promoted, and give that page its own og:image ('Stay on the ride, or get off?'). (Benchmark #2 Spoiler-free result card — Wordle)

[Kit: Assumption footer] Label the track 'a made-up fund's prices, to show the idea', and under every ending write '(made-up prices; real markets can fall further and take longer to recover; nothing is guaranteed)'. Frame the top-up choice as 'only if you have spare money and an emergency fund already in place', not as the winning move. Never show a fund name.

games.title: ChaiBoss Ltd — killer upgrade
games.verdict: You don't watch ChaiBoss, you run it. Each quarter you make a boss decision (launch a ₹10 kulhad chai, open five cities, pay the first dividend, quietly cut the milk), then drag a needle to predict what the market does to your share price. The reveal pours the answer into a chai glass: the tea level is profit per share and the steam is market mood. The screenshot moment is the twist quarter, 'Profits up 20%. Share price DOWN 6%. The market expected 30%.', with your needle pointing the wrong way.
games.share_idea: ☕ *ChaiBoss Ltd*: I ran a chai company for 8 quarters and called the share price 🎯🎯☕🎯❌🎯☕❌. Profits went UP and the price went DOWN. Can you work out why? 👇 games.investingformummies.com/classic?open=game7 _(made-up company, education only, not advice)_
games.share_moment: Your chai company just made record profits. So why did the share price fall? Run ChaiBoss for 8 quarters · 4 minutes

items.text: Make the intro's promise true: you run the company. Each quarter has two beats. First, a boss decision with a trade-off, for example Q2 when a rival launches cheaper chai: 'Cut your price to ₹8' (profit per share falls) or 'Stay premium and advertise' (costs now, mood holds). Second, the market reacts. Some quarters are news you cannot control (a rate cut, milk prices). The decisions change your share's path, and the greedy choice can backfire: cutting milk quality lifts this quarter's profit, then a viral complaint crushes mood the next quarter. (Anti-pattern 'Trivia dressed up as a game'; Benchmark #7 Teach in the result, not before the choice — SPENT)

[Kit: Feedback callout + off-by pill + "your guess, put to work"] Replace the A/B/C answers with a price needle. After each headline, the player drags a needle on a ₹50 to ₹250 dial to predict the new share price. The real price swings in over it with an off-by pill: within ₹10 is 🎯, within ₹25 is ☕, further off is ❌. A needle cannot show 'always option A', so the answer-position problem goes away by design, and every guess teaches the size of the move, not just its direction. (Benchmark #1 Guess first, then reveal — NYT You Draw It)

Add the 'priced in' twist quarter that the whole game builds towards: 'Record quarter: profit per share up 20%!' Most players drag the needle up. Then the reveal: analysts had expected 30%, mood drops from 14 to 11, and the price falls about 6% (₹168 to ₹158). A two-line callout explains why ('the share price already contained the good news everyone expected'). This is the counter-intuitive moment people will forward, and it is the share hook. (Benchmark #5 A dare that challenges the player's self-image — SPENT)

[Kit: Count-up + Sound] Show Price = Profit per share × Mood as a chai glass, not four number tiles. The tea level is profit per share in ₹, the steam height is the mood multiplier, and the price label on the glass counts up or down as both change. A pour animates when profit rises, steam puffs when mood rises and fades when it falls, and a kettle whistle plays on big moves. The formula line under it ('₹12 × 11 = ₹132') stays, but now the picture explains it. (Benchmark #12 Juice — Juice it or lose it)

Rename the jargon on screen: EPS becomes 'Profit per share (EPS)' and P/E becomes 'Mood multiplier (P/E): investors pay ₹11 for every ₹1 of yearly profit'. Keep the four 'What is…?' chips, but attach each to the number it explains instead of a row above the story. Use sentence case and buttons that say what you get ('Set my price →', 'Next quarter →'). Retire 'Let's Brew Some Profits ☕ →' and the grade titles ('Stock Market Star!', 'Growing Your Knowledge!').

[Kit: Result rows + Personal best] End on an 'Annual report' card styled like a company report: the 8-quarter price line with the player's needle guesses as dots, and three rows. 'Mood moved your price more than profit in 5 of 8 quarters.' 'Best call: the rate-cut rally.' 'The one that fooled you: record profits, falling price.' Headline it with an archetype: The Mood Reader, The Numbers Purist (followed profit, missed mood) or The Eternal Optimist (always guessed up). Add one tailored line and a personal best. (Benchmark #10 End on an identity — How Bad Is Your Spotify)

For replay, deal one of three made-up companies at random: ChaiBoss, DosaDost Foods and Kulfi Cart Co. Each has a different order of events and a different twist (for example, bad news everyone expected, so the price rises; or a dividend quarter where the price dips on the payout date). 'Good news means up' then stops being a winning strategy, and a second play teaches something new. (Benchmark #15 Same game, one variable changed — NGPF PAYBACK)

[Kit: Top bar + Title block + Primary / sticky / outline / WhatsApp buttons] On its own page, use the intro shape: kicker '8 QUARTERS · 4 MINUTES', title 'Chai*Boss* Ltd', the hook, and 'Open the shop →'. Play goes one screen per beat (headline → decision → needle → reveal), with Price · Profit/share · Mood in one slim sticky row in the top bar instead of the tall stacked navy pills seen live on a phone. Remove the doubled 'The ChaiBoss Challenge' header and the classic page's floating Menu / Suggest pills.

games.verdict: Make the player the fourth investor. Lucky, Steady and Worried race through 26 real years of the Nifty 50 index, and you race beside them with the same ₹1 lakh a year. At each crash (2000, 2008, 2011, 2020) you choose: keep going, skip a year, or sell everything for an FD. The screenshot moment is the four-lane finish: Worried Waris, who bought at the top every single year, ends on about ₹1.49 crore, while someone who sold once in 2008 ends on about ₹94 lakh. The unluckiest investor beats the panic seller by more than ₹50 lakh.

items.text: Add a fourth lane: 'You'. Today the player only watches. The killer version gives you the same ₹1 lakh every January, and each crash card (2000, 2008, 2011, 2020) asks 'Your money just fell 30%. What do you do?' with three big buttons: 'Keep investing', 'Skip next year (keep it in savings)' and 'Sell everything, move to an FD'. With the game's own data, staying in ends at about ₹1.88 Cr (same as Steady). Selling once at the end of 2008 (sold money and the 2009 instalment into an FD at 7%, investing again from 2010) ends at about ₹94 L. Skipping the year after every down year (that money kept in savings at 4%) ends at about ₹1.40 Cr. (Benchmark #8 Compress decades into minutes — NGPF STAX; #14 Desperate lifelines with a hidden price — SPENT)

[Kit: Feedback callout + off-by pill + "your guess, put to work"] Before the result, ask for a guess: 'Lucky bought at every year's lowest point. Waris bought at every year's highest. Drag to guess how much more Lucky ended with.' The slider runs from ₹0 to ₹2 Cr. Then reveal about ₹74 L more (₹2.22 Cr vs ₹1.49 Cr), and a second line: 'Steady, who just invested every January with zero effort, was about ₹34 L behind perfect, and nobody can actually do what Lucky did.' That makes the realistic choice Steady versus panic, which is the honest lesson. (Benchmark #1 Guess first, then reveal — NYT You Draw It)

[Kit: Money formatting + Count-up] Talk in rupees, not CAGR. Every card, the chart axis (today labelled 5.8%, 10.1%, 12.5%, 14.2%) and the result heroes show only annualised % returns, which most mums cannot picture. Lead with the rupee value counting up ('₹1.88 Cr from ₹26 L put in') and show the % as a quiet second line ('about 12.7% a year'). The current headline 'the CAGR gap is just 2.3% per year' should become 'Perfect timing vs worst timing: about ₹74 L apart. Panicking once: about ₹94 L behind staying put.'

Rebuild the crash card for a phone. Today it lays out the title, three investor cards, 'Why this matters' and the button side by side, so on a 390 px screen the lesson is squeezed into a column about one word wide and runs off the card (seen live on the 2000 Dot-com card). Stack it instead: headline and one line on what happened, the four lane values, a two-line lesson, then the three decision buttons, 56 px tall, in the thumb zone. Raise the 0.42–0.5 rem (7–8 px) labels to at least 12 px.

[Kit: Sound + Count-up] Turn the line chart into a four-lane race. Each investor is a token (🍀 Lucky, 📅 Steady, 😰 Waris, ⭐ You) climbing a lane whose height is the portfolio's value, with a year ticker from 1996 to 2021 and a newspaper headline that flips for each event. Crash years shake the lanes with a soft low thud, recoveries chime, and a faint dashed fifth lane shows 'all 26 lakh in an FD at 7%: about ₹74 L', so 'the real risk is not being invested' is finally visible rather than just asserted. Keep the whole run to about 60 seconds by default. (Benchmark #6 One live number you can't stop watching — SPENT; #12 Juice)

[Kit: Result rows + Life bar / timeline] End on a 'four lanes' card: rupee totals for all four investors with yours highlighted, and a timeline strip marking the years you skipped or sold, each labelled with what it cost compared with staying in. Head it with a kind archetype and one next step: The Statue (never flinched), The Skipper, or The Bailout ('Write down today what you'll do in the next crash, then wait 30 days before acting on a scary headline'). Replace the three takeaway paragraphs in 10 px type. (Benchmark #10 End on an identity — BitLife; #17 One personal sentence as the answer — NYT rent-or-buy)

Add replays that change one thing. 'Replay without selling' reruns the same 26 years with your sells turned into stays and shows both lanes side by side. 'Start in 2007' begins at the peak just before the 2008 crash, the scariest possible start. Using the game's data to 2021, ₹1 lakh every January from 2007 (₹15 L in total) still reaches about ₹41 L for Steady and about ₹33 L for Waris, against about ₹27 L in a 7% FD. (Benchmark #15 Same game, one variable changed — NGPF PAYBACK)

[Kit: Top bar + Title block + Primary / sticky / outline / WhatsApp buttons] On its own page, use the intro shape: kicker '26 YEARS · 4 CRASHES · 3 MINUTES', title 'The Timing *Trap*', the hook as a dare, the three rivals as small tokens, and 'Take your seat →'. That way the first tap is a seat in the race, not a setup table. Leave behind the classic page's banner and the floating Menu / Suggest pills that cover the controls. (Benchmark #3 First tap is the first decision — SPENT, Wordle)

[Kit: WhatsApp share (text) + Share image card] The WhatsApp line is one emoji per crash (✅ stayed, ⏭️ skipped, 🏃 sold) plus where you finished against Waris, with no rupee amounts. The 9:16 card shows the four lanes as a podium. Link to the game's own page once promoted, and give it an og:image reading 'The unluckiest investor still made crores. Can you beat him?' (Benchmark #2 Spoiler-free result card — Wordle; #4 Link preview as the cover)

[Kit: Assumption footer] A market index (not a single stock or fund) is fine to use, but every rupee figure needs its basis on screen and in the share: 'Nifty 50 price index, excludes dividends, before tax and costs; FD assumed 7% a year; past returns are not a promise.' Rename the takeaway 'Crashes are the best buying opportunities' to 'In these 26 years, every crash was followed by a recovery, so staying put mattered more than timing'. Tag Lucky 'Nobody can do this. He's here to measure the gap.' Recompute every number above when the data is extended past 2021.
